limitations: Conditions claims (wave height, wind, swell, current, water temp, tide windows) are sourced from peer-reviewed forecast and reanalysis models — they are statistically calibrated but not site-specific to the metre. Tropical-cyclone history is from IBTrACS. None of this replaces a local operator's morning briefing. We use these for climatological 'what to expect in this month' framing, not day-of dive go/no-go calls.

Pollution and water-quality claims are sourced from governmental monitoring networks and peer-reviewed registries — coverage is excellent in the US, EU, and Australia and patchier elsewhere. Microplastic concentrations vary enormously by time, season, and depth — published values are sparse spatial averages. Harmful algal bloom forecasts are short-term (days to weeks) and species-specific. Always confirm current advisories with the local operator before relying on this layer for site selection.

Bathymetry comes from GEBCO at 15-arcsecond global resolution — good for depth context but not survey-grade for navigation. Wreck history is taken from naval / governmental archives (DANFS, ENC Direct, NOAA Maritime Heritage) which are authoritative for cited vessels but do not cover every sport-dive wreck worldwide. Volcanic and seismic context (Smithsonian GVP, USGS) is event-level — use for 'this site sits near an active fault / volcano' framing, not for risk assessment.

The MPA status shown on each reef (no-take, strict, multi-use, none) is currently an editorial classification by region, informed by published Protected Planet (WDPA) and Marine Protection Atlas designations rather than pulled live from them; a direct MPAtlas/WDPA ingest is in progress. Not every MPA is genuinely enforced, which is why we distinguish paper-park designations from no-take protection. Fishing pressure, by contrast, is measured: it comes from Global Fishing Watch AIS data within 50 kilometres of each location, so it reflects vessels near a reef rather than inside a single dive zone, and it captures industrial vessels but misses small-scale and illegal fishing. We show this apparent fishing effort as a trend across several years, not a single snapshot. Where that trend is falling next to a protected reef, we read it as fishing pressure easing, a supporting signal that protection may be taking hold and a complement to the fish-biomass recovery story. It is context, not proof of enforcement: fishing near a marine protected area is often legal outside a small no-take core, and any vessel that does not broadcast AIS stays invisible, so a falling line is never an enforcement accusation. We use these layers for context — not to certify that a specific site is well-managed or fish-stocked. Always confirm permits and rules with the local operator before booking.

Trip-cost estimates are editorial ranges, not live prices. Flight ranges reflect typical round-trip economy fares from each regional hub during the location's dive season; off-season or last-minute fares often fall outside. Lodging tiers are per-night ranges for double-occupancy mid-week stays — peak holiday weeks (Easter, Christmas/New Year, Chinese New Year) commonly run 20–50% higher. Dive-day prices assume a 2-boat-dive package with tanks/weights/guide included and exclude private guide, nitrox, and equipment rental. We do not claim accuracy beyond ±15%; book operators directly to confirm.

Observed coral cover, bleaching, and mortality come from named in-situ surveys with a stated date and method — they describe one snapshot of one reef and do not extrapolate to neighbouring sites. Current thermal stress is satellite-derived from NOAA Coral Reef Watch at ~5 km resolution; it indicates risk, not observed coral damage. We deliberately separate observed condition, current thermal stress, and projection — and we never publish a projection without a documented model and uncertainty.

We aggregate confirmed occurrence records from GBIF and OBIS within a fixed radius of each dive site. Occurrence records confirm presence and reveal seasonality clustering, but they DO NOT measure per-dive probability — there is no eligible-effort denominator. We deliberately do not publish a numeric '% chance of sighting' from this data.

Best months are derived from clustering of occurrence records and operator-reported seasons. No per-trip probability is published — the Sardine Run varies year to year with current and water temperature.
Regional populations have shifted; operator availability changes annually. We do not publish per-trip probability.
Schooling behavior is operator-reported. Aggregation density varies with current, lunar phase, and temperature.
Best months are derived from occurrence-record clustering and well-documented regional aggregations. Per-trip probability is not published.
Cleaning stations are site-specific; visit frequency varies with current and time of day.
Monad Shoal threshers are reliably present year-round but encounters are pre-dawn and weather-dependent. No per-dive probability.
Aggregation timing shifts with water temperature and prey. Encounter is occurrence-clustered, not survey-measured.
Subject diversity is highly variable. We do not list per-species probabilities for blackwater dives.
Exact spawning night varies by reef and year. Predictions are operator-tracked and affected by ocean temperature anomalies.
Daily ascent is consistent at established rubble sites but very brief; not a guarantee on any single dive.
Aggregation numbers fluctuate; the Spencer Gulf population crashed in the 2010s and has only partially recovered.

calculation: Hard coral cover % taken from percent_cover_benthic_category_avg["Hard coral"] in the MERMAID summarysampleevents endpoint. Benthic PIT preferred over LIT over photo-quadrat when multiple protocols exist for the same event. Most recent survey event within 0.5° of location centre used.
limitations: Survey events are matched by geographic proximity (0.5° radius), not by explicit dive site name — a survey at a nearby site may not perfectly represent the named location. Cover is the mean across all sample units in that survey event. Older surveys may not reflect post-bleaching changes.

This is a regional benchmark, not a reading of the reef you are looking at. The numbers are mean indicator-fish densities across all Reef Check belt transects in an ocean basin (the Indo-Pacific or the Atlantic and Caribbean) over 1997 to 2001, so they show a basin-wide direction, not the state of a single site. Reef Check counts a fixed set of indicator families (grouper, snapper, sweetlips, parrotfish, humphead wrasse, butterflyfish) rather than all fish, and volunteer counts carry more observer variance than professional surveys. We show it because those same standardised counts found five of ten indicator groups significantly more abundant inside marine protected areas than outside, which is honest, effort-standardised evidence that protection rebuilds fish. It never drives a location's reef-state verdict.

Fish abundance comes from in-situ belt-transect surveys (underwater visual census) at named monitoring stations, reported per 500 m² by the survey program, and is display-only context that does not set the reef-state verdict. We show published start-versus-end values for each station rather than a smoothed line because the full year-by-year data is held by the programs and released on request; reading points off a plotted figure would not be real data. Different programs use different methods, units and fish groupings and must not be spliced into one series. Target and commercial families track fishing and protection well; total-fish counts also swing with schooling species and storms, so we report the counter-evidence alongside the trend.

calculation: Per REEF geographic zone and calendar year, the community abundance index is the sighting-frequency-weighted mean density across all reported species: Σ(%SF·DEN)/Σ(%SF), where %SF is a species' sighting frequency (surveys recording it / total surveys) and DEN is its density score (mean of the Roving Diver Technique abundance categories Single=1, Few=2, Many=3, Abundant=4 across surveys recording it), bounded 1–4. Only years with at least 10 Species-&-Abundance surveys are kept, and a location needs at least 3 such years to publish a series. The number of surveys behind each year is stored and shown as the effort denominator. Trend is the sign of the least-squares slope of the index over years, with a 0.15 (on the 1–4 scale) deadband.
limitations: This is a RELATIVE abundance index from volunteer surveys, not biomass and not a fish count. It is recorded at REEF geographic-zone resolution (a zone can span many dive sites), so it never represents a single site and never feeds the reef-state verdict — it is a display-only trend. Density categories are log-scaled and coarse (four bins). Observer skill varies between volunteers; this index pools expert and novice surveyors. Survey effort is uneven across years and zones, so sparse years are dropped rather than shown. Scoped to regions where REEF coverage is strong (Tropical Western Atlantic/Caribbean, US, Tropical Eastern Pacific); not applied where REEF coverage is thin (Mediterranean, Indo-Pacific).

calculation: Live-coral cover % from LCAVG and total fish biomass (g/100 m², displayed as kilograms per hectare via a lossless ×0.1 conversion) from FBIOMASS in the AGRRA Data Explorer BaseBySite FeatureServer, both filtered to >= 0 to drop the -999 no-data sentinel. Survey sites are grouped into one mean value per survey year. Scope is proximity first — all AGRRA sites within 0.75° (~83 km) of the location centre — falling back to the location's own-country national composite only when proximity yields fewer than three survey years AND the nearest same-country AGRRA site is within 1.5°. A coral series is published only when it spans at least three survey years; the fish series is carried when it spans at least two.
limitations: AGRRA is a rapid-assessment programme: sites are not resurveyed on a fixed annual schedule, so survey years are uneven and some gaps are multi-year. Values are proximity or national composites matched to our location centres, not the exact dive site, and the annual mean pools every surveyed site in that scope. These trend charts are display-only: they never set the reef-state verdict or the headline coral-cover number, which stay on the hand-reviewed reef-health record. Reef Life Survey is the primary fish-biomass source; the AGRRA fish series is shown only where RLS has no coverage, and the two use different survey methods so absolute biomass levels are not comparable across sources (within-site trend direction is what the chart conveys).

calculation: Standing reef-fish biomass from Reef Life Survey Method 1 (M1) underwater visual transects, served by the IMOS AODN geoserver (imos:ep_m1_public_data). For each M1 survey, fish biomass is summed across all species and size classes within each 50 m x 5 m (250 m²) transect block, converted to a density in kilograms per hectare (grams per block x 0.04), and averaged across the survey's blocks so the figure is robust to whether one or two blocks were surveyed. A location's value for a year is the mean survey density across all M1 surveys within 0.5° (~55 km) of the location centre in that year, so a run of surveys becomes a real trend line. Every point is an observed value; nothing is projected. Latest-year abundance and species richness are the mean fish count per standard 500 m² transect and the mean distinct fish species per transect.
limitations: Surveys are matched by proximity (0.5° radius), not by exact dive site, so nearby transects may not perfectly represent the named location. This is a DISPLAY-ONLY trend chart and never sets the reef-state label. RLS coverage is uneven: strong on temperate, Mediterranean and long-running Australian reefs, but sparse or absent across much of the tropical Indo-Pacific, and many reefs are surveyed only once (no trend, so no chart). Biomass is estimated from visual size-class to weight conversions and can spike when a single large school or big-bodied fish is recorded on a transect. Volunteer (RLS) and professional (ATRC and partner) M1 surveys are pooled by shared method.

These are peer-reviewed reef fish biomass findings for individual Blue Park sites, each comparing protected water against fished water (inside versus outside) or protection over time (before versus after), with the headline figure quoted as published. We use fish biomass as the signal that protection is working, which is distinct from coral condition: coral loss on these reefs is driven by marine heat, not by fishing. Where a reef is a documented biomass recovery and its coral is not currently falling, we set the reef state to Improving on this basis (for example Channel Islands, Abrolhos, Chumbe, alongside Torre Guaceto). Where the coral is currently declining under heat, we keep the coral-driven reef state and show the biomass finding as context rather than labelling the reef Improving. Two figures (Chumbe, Kisite-Mpunguti) were confirmed through the peer-reviewed Conservation Evidence synthesis of the primary studies rather than the paywalled primary PDF. Standing stock benchmarks without a fished control (Darwin and Wolf, Malpelo, Cocos, Aldabra) show an intact protected reef rather than a measured before-and-after recovery.

calculation: For locations with no on-site reef survey, live-coral cover % is the pooled per-survey-year mean of LCAVG from the AGRRA Data Explorer BaseBySite FeatureServer, filtered to >= 0 to drop the -999 no-data sentinel. Scope is proximity first — every AGRRA site within 0.75° (~83 km) of the location centre — falling back to the location's own-country national composite only when proximity yields fewer than three survey years AND the nearest same-country AGRRA site is within 1.5°. The latest survey year sets the headline coral-cover number and the earliest sets the historical baseline; a record is created only when the series spans at least three survey years. Thermal stress is added separately by the daily NOAA CRW job.
limitations: Unlike an on-site survey, these values are a nearby AGRRA composite matched to the location centre, so they describe the surrounding reef area rather than the exact dive site, and the annual mean pools every surveyed station in scope. They are used to give an otherwise-unsurveyed location a real, honestly-sourced reef-state instead of leaving it blank; a location's record is upgraded to a curated on-site survey whenever one becomes available. Every number is a real AGRRA survey value — none is modelled or estimated. Confidence is medium (not high) precisely because the survey is near the location, not at it.

calculation: Stony coral cover per station-year is the sum of ID_Percent_Cover across every row whose ID_Group is Stony_Coral in the CREMP point-count export (the raw column is a fraction, so it is multiplied by 100). A station that was surveyed but recorded no stony coral counts as a real zero, not as missing data. Station values are averaged within a monitoring site, then site means are averaged to the published value, so a site with more stations does not outweigh the others. Reefs are keyed on the numeric Site id rather than name, because the five Palm Beach reefs were relabelled from subregion PBC to PB in 2025. For a regional series only reefs monitored in at least 95% of that region's survey years are pooled, so a falling trend cannot be an artifact of reefs joining the programme later; where a region is too young or too patchy for such a panel, every reef on record is used and the chart caption says so. A dive-site series pools only the CREMP station sets that sit on that exact reef.
limitations: CREMP measures stony coral cover at fixed stations, a different design from the stratified-random NOAA NCRMP surveys, so values are not directly comparable between the two programmes. For the Florida Keys the CREMP figures are also what the reef-health record now cites: they match the published record for the reef tract (about 12% cover in 1996 falling to roughly 5% by 2015), whereas the NCRMP-attributed pair they replaced did not. The regional value pools whole monitoring regions, so it describes the region rather than any one dive site, and only Molasses Reef and Looe Key Reef have an exact same-reef series. Cover is the stony-coral group only; octocorals, sponges and macroalgae are in the source data but are not charted. These trend charts are display-only: they never set the reef-state verdict or the headline coral-cover number, which stay on the hand-reviewed reef-health record. The 2025 values come from a direct data transfer from FWRI and are not yet on the public FWC download.
